In brief

The first half of Nausicaa ends when Gerty walks off after her friends "with a certain quiet dignity characteristic of her but with care and very slowly," because, as Bloom thinks when his familiar interior monologue returns, "Tight boots? No. She's lame! O!" This realization casts a whole new light on the preceding voyeuristic interaction, though alert readers may have caught a reference to it in Gerty's thoughts some paragraphs earlier. Together the two passages make clear that Gerty's physical defect is making her a spinster. 

At more length

Before the lewd flirtation begins in earnest, Gerty has mused ethereally on the beauties of the summer evening and on paintings, novels, poems, diaries, colored inks. The "transient loveliness" of poetry makes her cry because it reminds her that "the years were slipping by for her, one by one, and but for that one shortcoming she knew she need fear no competition and that was an accident coming down Dalkey hill and she always tried to conceal it." This is the first indication that Gerty is starting to get on in years and that a physical flaw has damaged her marriage prospects. When Bloom's thoughts take over, both his compassion and his crudely objectifying sexual responses underline the point: "Mr Bloom watched her as she limped away. Poor girl! That's why she's left on the shelf and the others did a sprint. Thought something was wrong by the cut of her jib. Jilted beauty. A defect is ten times worse in a woman. But makes them polite. Glad I didn't know it when she was on show. Hot little devil all the same. I wouldn't mind. Curiosity like a nun or a negress or a girl with glasses."

Gifford notes that "Gerty's lameness may be much more of a disadvantage than she allows, given both male attitudes toward women in 1904 (Dublin) and the strikingly low marriage rate." The introduction to his annotations notes the paucity of good alternatives to marriage or convent life available to middle-class women in 1904 Dublin, and the fact that "Marriage itself was by no means something that could be expected in due course" (6). Ireland's population plummeted after the Great Hunger of the 1840s, as did its marriage and birth rates. "In 1901 more than 80 percent of men between twenty-five and thirty years of age and more than 60 percent between thirty and thirty-five were unmarried" (6). Women stood a less than 50-50 chance of ever finding a spouse—and the odds would have steadily declined after their prime years of sexual attractiveness. A physical defect would hardly help matters.

Gerty's lameness, then, sheds poignant light on her eagerness to find a husband. Her fantasies of marrying a 17-year-old boy or (minutes later) a much older stranger that she sees on a beach smack of desperation. In this way Nausicaa hearkens back to the stories of Dubliners, with their searing portraits of people trapped in dead-end lives. Many of the doomed people in those stories are female: the girl torn between familial duty and a little-known man's promises in "Eveline"; the wife shackled to an abusive alcoholic in "A Boarding House"; the mother laboring to make a name for her daughter in "A Mother"; the spinster toiling in a laundry in "Clay." The portrait of Gerty feels much less bleak, its element of sexual vitality lifting it out of the religious, moral, and paternalistic morass of Dubliners. But this final detail lowers a gate on Gerty with a loud clang, just as the endings of Joyce's early stories do to person after hopeful person.

John Hunt 2026
